title: Wound care when reaching is hard with arthritis and frailty (UK)
meta_title: Wound care when reaching is hard with arthritis and frailty
meta_description: Wound care when arthritis makes reaching hard: clean minor cuts, plan dressing help and recognise wounds that need urgent or emergency care.
excerpt: When arthritis makes a wound hard to see or reach, get a workable dressing plan. Learn minor-cut care, what to ask the practice and when to seek urgent help.
direct_answer: For a small cut, first stop any bleeding, then clean and cover it. If arthritis makes reaching unsafe, ask for help and tell your GP practice which tasks you cannot manage. Uncontrolled bleeding, deep wounds, loss of feeling or an embedded object need emergency assessment. Infection signs need urgent advice.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: wound care, cuts, legs, feet, arthritis, frailty, community nurse, infection, UK

citations.label: NHS: Skin infection symptoms and urgent help

content:
When sore hands, stiff hips or poor balance make a wound hard to reach, the problem is not simply remembering to change a dressing. You may be unable to see whether it is clean, keep a dressing dry or get into a safe position. A small cut can need practical help even when it does not need emergency treatment.

This guide from Living With Arthritis explains basic care for a minor cut or graze and how to ask for help when reaching is difficult. It is not a dressing plan for a surgical wound, pressure ulcer, diabetic foot wound or long-standing leg ulcer. Follow the instructions from the team treating those wounds.

Quick answer: what should you do first?

First check for bleeding or features that need urgent treatment. Once bleeding has stopped, a small cut can usually be rinsed with clean water and covered with a sterile dressing. If you cannot see or reach it safely, ask for help rather than twisting, standing on one leg or guessing. Contact your GP practice if you need an assessment or help arranging ongoing wound care.

When does a wound need emergency help?

The NHS cuts and grazes guide advises calling 999 or going to A&E for a cut with any of the following:

  • Bleeding you cannot stop, or bright red blood coming out in spurts that is hard to control.
  • Loss of feeling near the wound or difficulty moving the injured area.
  • A very large or deep wound, or a bad cut on the face or palm.
  • Something embedded in the wound, such as glass. Do not pull it out yourself.

Do not drive yourself to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance. Do not delay emergency help while trying to arrange a routine dressing appointment.

How can you care for a small cut or graze?

These steps apply after bleeding has stopped, when there are no emergency features. The NHS describes cleaning and covering the wound to reduce the risk of infection.

  1. Wash and dry your hands. Use disposable gloves if available.
  2. Rinse the small wound with tap or bottled water, or use sterile wipes. Do not dig into it to remove an embedded object.
  3. Gently dry the area with clean gauze or a clean cloth. Cover the wound while cleaning the surrounding skin with soap and water, wiping away from the wound.
  4. Remove that temporary covering and apply a sterile plaster or dressing.
  5. Keep the dressing clean and dry. Change it when needed, rather than leaving a wet or dirty dressing in place. For a simple cut, the NHS says the dressing can be removed after a few days once the wound has closed.

If the wound is bleeding, use a clean folded cloth or bandage to apply pressure, provided there is no object stuck in it. If an object is embedded, do not press on it or remove it. Seek emergency help. The NHS page linked above gives further first-aid instructions.

Practical tip: Put clean supplies within reach before starting. If you cannot finish the task safely, stop and ask for help. A difficult position is not made safer by hurrying.

What if arthritis makes the dressing difficult?

Explain the part of the task that is failing. “I cannot reach my ankle” is useful, but “I cannot see the wound, open the packet or keep the dressing in place” gives the practice more information about the help you need.

A stable seated position may be more manageable than standing. Do not use a wheeled chair or balance on furniture to reach a leg or foot. If you cannot find a safe position, ask another person for practical help or contact the practice. A mirror can help you look at an area, but it does not make a deep or infected wound suitable for self-treatment.

You can ask a pharmacist about dressings for a minor wound. Ask the GP practice whether a nurse or another clinician should assess it if you are unsure what it needs. Do not assume every wound can be managed by changing the type of plaster.

Who can help with wound care at home?

Tell your GP practice if you cannot attend or cannot manage wound care because of mobility, hand function, eyesight or another health problem. Ask what assessment and referral options are available locally. Community nursing arrangements and access criteria vary. Being housebound does not by itself confirm a particular service or guarantee a home visit.

If you already have a wound-care team, use its contact details and dressing plan. Before a planned visit ends, check who will provide supplies, who will change the next dressing and whom to contact if the wound changes. If the arrangement is not workable, say so before you run out of dressings or miss a change.

For example, someone may be able to attend a clinic with transport but still be unable to remove an ankle dressing between appointments. That needs to be part of the plan, not left as an assumed task for a relative. Agree what any helper is comfortable doing and leave treatment decisions to the clinical team.

Which changes need an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111?

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if a cut becomes swollen, red and increasingly painful, or pus appears. Redness may be less obvious on brown or black skin, so also notice swelling, warmth, pain and discharge. Seek urgent advice if you feel generally unwell or have a high temperature after a cut.

The NHS also recommends urgent assessment when a wound remains dirty after cleaning, contains soil or body fluids, follows a bite from a person or a wild or stray animal, or is larger than about 5cm. Something firmly embedded in a cut belongs on the emergency route above, not a home-cleaning attempt.

In England, Scotland and Wales, call 111 for urgent advice when appropriate. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. Emergency symptoms need 999 or A&E instead.

When should tetanus protection be checked?

A wound can need a tetanus assessment even when it seems small. Ask your GP practice or urgent-care service if you have not been fully vaccinated or do not know your vaccination history, particularly after a dirty wound. The NHS tetanus guide explains the risks and when to seek help. Do not wait for symptoms before asking whether protection is needed.

What should you record for the nurse or GP?

  • When and how the wound happened, including a bite, fall or dirty object.
  • Changes in pain, swelling, discharge, bleeding or feeling around it.
  • What cleaning and dressings have already been used.
  • Which parts of care you cannot manage and whether someone can help.
  • Your medicines, relevant conditions and any existing wound-care instructions.

This is a conversation aid, not a home test for infection. Do not delay urgent care to build a diary or take photographs.

Remember: A photograph or diary can help describe a change, but cannot rule out infection or replace examination.

Key takeaways

  • Use basic cleaning and a sterile dressing only for a minor wound without emergency features.
  • Say which parts of wound care are impossible or unsafe, so the plan does not depend on help you do not have.
  • Use urgent or emergency care for the symptoms above rather than waiting for a routine dressing visit.

Frequently asked questions

Can a district nurse dress every wound at home?

No universal arrangement can be promised. Ask your practice about assessment, local criteria and alternatives if you cannot attend.

Should I remove a wet dressing?

For a minor cut, keep the dressing clean and dry and change it when needed. For a wound being treated by a clinical team, follow its plan and contact it if the dressing becomes wet or will not stay in place.

Can a relative help?

A willing helper may assist with supplies or a simple dressing, but should not probe a wound, remove an embedded object or choose treatment for a worsening wound. Ask for a clear clinical plan if care is ongoing.

Should I wait until the next appointment if it looks infected?

No. Increasing pain, swelling, pus or feeling unwell needs urgent advice rather than waiting for the next routine dressing change.

Does this guide apply to a new diabetic foot wound?

No. A new diabetic foot problem needs prompt contact with your diabetes foot team or GP. Emergency features need immediate assessment. Use the related diabetic-foot guide alongside your team's instructions.

Your next step

Check whether your immediate need is emergency treatment, urgent assessment or practical help with a minor wound. If reaching is the problem, tell the practice exactly what you cannot do. Read our related guidance on pressure care and diabetic feet without assuming that every wound has the same cause or treatment.
